title: Black Friday Customer Score
subtitle: How well can you tell which of your Black Friday buyers were worth paying for, scored across customer data, order margins, ad targets and repeat follow-up.

questions.text: Can you pull a list of every customer whose first order with you came in last year's Black Friday week?

answers.label: No. Guest checkout and our exports make it impossible to separate them
Someone could build it by hand from order exports in about a day
Yes, though returning customers who used a new email show up as new
Yes, it sits as a saved segment in our shop platform or email tool
Yes, the segment updates itself and sits next to last year's full-price group

questions.text: When a Black Friday buyer orders again in March, does anything in your setup know it is the same person?

answers.label: No, every order is a separate line in the export
Only if they log into an account, and few of them do
We match on email, so a different email or a guest order breaks the link
We match on email and phone and clean duplicates every quarter
One customer record across shop, email and ads, with each person's full order history

questions.text: Can you see, per customer, which Black Friday offer they used (the deepest code, free delivery, pay later)?

answers.label: No, discount data stays at order level and nobody looks at it
We see one total for discounts given that week
We can see the code on each order, and we never look at those buyers again
We tag buyers by the offer they used and check them at least once after the sale
We compare repeat orders by offer type, and it changes what we offer next year

questions.text: Do you know which Black Friday orders came back as returns, and who sent them?

answers.label: We don't track returns by week or by campaign
We know the total refunded for November
We know the return rate for the week, with no customer names attached
Returns are tied to the customer and the order, and removed from revenue in our reports
Returns are tied to the customer, removed from revenue, and removed from what the ad accounts count as a sale

low.headline: You can't yet tell who you bought last week
low.text: Right now your Black Friday buyers and your loyal customers sit in the same pile. Until you can pull last year's discount-week buyers as one list, the report answers every question about whether the week paid off, and the report only counts the first order.
steps: Export every order from last year's Black Friday week and mark the emails that had never ordered before
Match orders on email and phone so a second order in March links back to the same person
Tag each buyer with the offer they used
Take returned orders out of that week's revenue figure

mid.headline: You have the list. Put it next to something
mid.text: You can find these customers. What's missing is a comparison. A list in the shop platform tells you very little until last year's discount-week group sits next to the people who bought at full price.
steps: Build two saved segments, first order in Black Friday week and first order at full price
Clean duplicates once a quarter so guest orders stop breaking the match
Add returns per customer to the same view

high.headline: Your data can answer the hard question
high.text: You can see who came in on the discount, what they used and whether they came back. Keep it this clean before the Christmas offers and the January sales add two more groups.
steps: Create a segment for each offer period this season before it goes live
Share the customer view with whoever sets the ad targets
Check the match rate after each sale so the segments stay accurate

questions.text: At full price, what percentage of the selling price is left after product cost and delivery?
questions.hint: A €100 product that costs €40 to buy and €8 to send leaves 52%. Leave ad spend out of this number.

questions.text: What was your main Black Friday discount, as a percentage off full price?
questions.hint: Use the discount most of your orders got, for example 30 for 30% off.

questions.text: Before the sale went live, did anyone work out what each discounted order would leave you after product, delivery and ads?

answers.label: No, we set the discount by looking at what competitors offered
We checked that we'd still sell above product cost
We checked product and delivery cost and left ad spend out
We worked out profit per order, ads included, for our top products
Every product in the sale had a profit-per-order figure, and the ones that lost money stayed out of the sale

questions.text: Where does your margin data live, and who on the ads side has seen it?

answers.label: In the owner's head, or in the accountant's file once a year
In a spreadsheet the person running the ads has never opened
Shared with the ads team as one average margin for the whole shop
Margin per product or category, shared with whoever sets the ad targets
Margin per product sits in the feed or the account, so the platforms can bid on it

low.headline: The discount may have cost you more than the report shows
low.text: On a €100 product that costs €40 to buy and €8 to send, 30% off at a 2.5 ROAS loses you €6 on every order. Nothing in Meta or Google shows that. If nobody worked this out before Black Friday, start with your ten best sellers now, before the Christmas offers go out.
steps: Write down product cost and delivery cost for your ten best sellers
Work out what each one leaves you at the discounted price, with ad spend included
Pull any product that loses money at that discount out of the next sale
Send the margin sheet to whoever runs your ads

mid.headline: You know the margin. The ads side needs it too
mid.text: One average margin for the whole shop hides the products that lose money on every discounted order. Break it down by product or category, and make sure the person setting targets has actually seen it.
steps: Split margin by product or category for everything in the next sale
Mark the products that fall below break-even at the planned discount
Review the sheet with your ads person before Christmas offers go live

high.headline: Your margins are ready to drive your bids
high.text: You know what every discounted order leaves you. The next step is getting that number into the accounts, so Google and Meta go looking for orders with profit in them.
steps: Add margin per product to your product feed or conversion values
Set a minimum margin for any product that enters a promotion
Recheck margins when supplier or courier prices change

questions.text: When did anyone last change the ROAS target your campaigns run on?

answers.label: I don't know what our target is
It was set when the account was built and nobody has touched it
We changed it this year, well before the discount season
We raised it for Black Friday week by what felt safe
We set a new target for every offer period, worked out from break-even ROAS at that price

questions.text: What does your ad account count as a conversion during Black Friday week?

answers.label: Any purchase event, including orders later refunded or cancelled
Purchases at the price the customer paid, with no cost data
Purchases, with refunds removed by hand later in a report
Purchases with margin or profit values sent back to the account
Profit values, plus a separate signal for new customers and returning ones

questions.text: Can your ad account tell a new customer from someone who already bought from you?

answers.label: No, every buyer looks the same to Google and Meta
We think so, someone switched a setting on once
We upload a customer list now and then, months old by the time it's used
Customer lists sync regularly and we bid differently for new customers
Lists sync automatically and we see what a new customer cost us, separate from returning ones

questions.text: When this year's Black Friday report came in, what did you look at first?

answers.label: Revenue and ROAS in the platform dashboard
Revenue against last year's Black Friday
Orders and cost per order, with returns still counted
Profit after product, delivery, ads and returns
Profit, plus how many buyers were new and what each new customer cost compared with October

low.headline: Your target was set for a price you no longer sell at
low.text: In my example, break-even ROAS moves from 1.92 at full price to 3.18 at 30% off. If your October target is still running, the account keeps spending to it and reports a good week. Check the target before every offer period.
steps: Find out what ROAS target each campaign runs on today
Work out break-even ROAS at the price you're selling at this month
Remove refunded and cancelled orders from what counts as a conversion
Read profit first when the next sale report comes in

mid.headline: The account counts sales. Feed it what you keep
mid.text: Your targets move with the season, and the account still only sees the price the customer paid. Feed it a sale with a margin attached and it starts finding more of those.
steps: Send profit or margin values back to Google and Meta
Sync your customer list so the account can tell new buyers from returning ones
Report cost per new customer next to ROAS every week of a sale

high.headline: Your account knows what a sale is worth
high.text: Targets reset with the price and the accounts bid on profit. Keep comparing what a new customer cost you in a discount week with a normal month, and use that gap to decide how deep the next discount goes.
steps: Recalculate break-even ROAS for the January sales before they launch
Compare cost per new customer in Black Friday week with October
Cap spend on campaigns that bring mostly returning buyers during a sale

questions.text: Of the customers whose first order came in last year's Black Friday week, what percentage have ordered again since?
questions.hint: If you can't pull this number, enter 0 and treat that as your answer.

questions.text: What happens to a Black Friday buyer in the 60 days after their first order?

answers.label: Nothing planned. They get the same newsletter as everyone
They get every promotion we send, mostly more discounts
A welcome email, then the regular newsletter
A separate follow-up flow with a reason to buy at full price
A separate flow, and we measure repeat orders and full-price share for that group against other buyers

questions.text: Have you ever compared the second orders of discount-week buyers with those of full-price buyers?

answers.label: No, it never came up
We've talked about it and nobody has pulled the data
We did it once, a while ago
Yes, for last year's Black Friday group
Yes, every year, and it decides how deep we go on the next sale

questions.text: Could you show your accountant today whether last year's Black Friday paid for itself nine months later?

answers.label: No, we'd only have the week's revenue
We could show the week's profit and nothing after it
We could estimate it, with a lot of guessing
Yes, with repeat orders counted from our own data
Yes, week profit plus repeat contribution per buyer, compared with full-price buyers

low.headline: You paid for customers you may never see again
low.text: In Sam Tomlinson's model, deep discounts brought 3.3x the orders, and 28 of the 32 extra buyers were never coming back. If your Black Friday buyers get the same newsletter as everyone else, you won't know which side of that number you're on until next November.
steps: Pull last year's Black Friday buyers and count how many ordered again
Set up a separate 60-day follow-up for this year's discount-week buyers
Give them a reason to buy at full price, like a product they haven't tried
Keep discount codes out of the first follow-up emails

mid.headline: You follow up. Now measure it
mid.text: A welcome email and a flow are a start. You still can't say whether this group buys again as often as your full-price customers, and you need that answer before deciding how deep the next sale goes.
steps: Compare repeat orders for discount-week buyers and full-price buyers at 90 days
Track what share of their second orders were at full price
Cut the flows that only send more discounts

high.headline: You can prove whether Black Friday paid off
high.text: You can put repeat contribution per buyer for the discount-week group next to your full-price buyers. That number belongs in the plan for next year's sale, before anyone picks a discount.
steps: Run the same comparison for this year's group in August, nine months after the sale
Share repeat contribution per buyer with whoever sets the discount
Test a shallower offer on part of next year's list and compare second orders

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.
